He then bowed and left. He saw nobody in the street at the time. It is a quiet, deserted side street.

“William Bird, a tailor, states that he was among those who entered the house. He is English and has lived in Paris for two years. He was one of the first to go upstairs and heard the arguing voices. The rough voice belonged to a Frenchman. He understood several words but cannot now remember them all. He clearly heard ‘sacré’ and ‘mon Dieu.’ At the same time, he heard scraping and scuffling, as though several people were struggling. The high-pitched voice was very loud, louder than the rough one. He is certain it was not an Englishman’s voice. It seemed to belong to a German, though it might have been a woman. He does not understand German.

“Four of the witnesses named above were recalled. They stated that the door to the room where Mademoiselle L.’s body was found was locked from inside when the group reached it. Everything was completely silent, without groans or any other sounds. After forcing the door open, they saw no one. The windows in both the front and back rooms were shut and firmly secured from within. The connecting door between the rooms was closed but unlocked. The door from the front room into the hallway was locked, with the key on the inside. A small room at the front of the house, on the fourth floor at the end of the hallway, stood partly open. It was packed with old beds, boxes, and other things, all of which were carefully moved and examined. Every inch of the house was thoroughly searched. Chimney sweeps were sent up and down the chimneys. The house had four floors and attic rooms. A trapdoor in the roof was securely nailed shut and appeared not to have been opened for years. Witnesses gave different estimates of the time between hearing the argument and breaking down the room’s door. Some said only three minutes; others said as many as five. The door was difficult to force open.

“Alfonzo Garcio, an undertaker, states that he lives in the Rue Morgue. He is Spanish by birth and was among those who entered the house. He did not go upstairs because he is nervous and feared what the excitement might do to him. He heard the arguing voices. The rough voice was French, though he could not make out the words. The high-pitched voice belonged to an Englishman; he is certain of this.

I turn now to my own story. There is little to tell about my earliest years, and I will keep it brief. But I must spend some time on my childhood, so that you can understand how the failure of a single hope could leave my whole life empty, and how the destruction of the only affection I was allowed to cherish extinguished my existence along with it.

I have already said that my aunt was very different from my father. I believe that, without the slightest trace of malice, she possessed the coldest heart ever carried in a human breast. It was entirely incapable of affection. She took me into her care because she believed it was her duty. But she had lived alone for too long, undisturbed by children's noise and chatter, to permit me to disrupt her peace. She had never married, and for the previous five years she had lived entirely alone on an estate inherited from her mother, beside Loch Lomond in Scotland. In his letters, my father had expressed a wish that she live with me at his family mansion, set in beautiful countryside near Richmond in Yorkshire. She refused. As soon as she had settled the affairs her brother's departure had left in her hands, she left England, taking me with her to her Scottish estate.

During my infancy and until I reached the age of eight, I was looked after by a servant of my mother's who had accompanied us into seclusion for that purpose. I lived in a remote part of the house and saw my aunt only at fixed times. This happened twice daily: once around noon, when she visited my nursery, and again after her dinner, when I was brought to her. She never showed me physical affection. Throughout my time in the room, she seemed afraid I would annoy her with some childish mischief. Before venturing into the parlor, my good nurse always coached me with the greatest care. My aunt's cold looks and few stiff words inspired such awe that I rarely betrayed my nurse's training or abandoned the exemplary stillness expected of me during these brief visits.

Under my kind nurse's supervision, I roamed freely through our park and the neighboring fields. Born of the deepest love, I showed extraordinary emotional sensitivity from my earliest years. I cannot describe how passionately I loved everything around me, even lifeless objects.

He shuddered and stepped back inside, shutting the window behind him.

At the door, he turned the key and opened it without so much as glancing at the murdered man. The secret of managing this, he felt, was to avoid taking in what had happened. The friend who had painted the fatal portrait, the source of all his misery, was gone from his life. That was enough.

Then he remembered the lamp. It was an unusual piece of Moorish craftsmanship, made of tarnished silver inlaid with flowing designs of polished steel and set with rough turquoises. His servant might notice it was missing and ask questions. He hesitated, then went back and lifted it from the table. He could not avoid seeing the dead thing. How motionless it was! How terribly white those long hands looked! It resembled a hideous wax figure.

He locked the door behind him and crept downstairs. The wood creaked, seeming to cry out in pain. Several times he stopped and waited. No, all was quiet. The only sound was his own footsteps.

In the library, he noticed the bag and coat in the corner. He had to hide them somewhere. He unlocked a concealed cupboard in the wall paneling, where he kept his own strange disguises, and put them inside. He could easily burn them later. Then he took out his watch. It was twenty to two.

He sat down to think. Every year—almost every month—men in England were hanged for what he had just done. A murderous madness must have been in the air. Some red star had passed too close to the earth.... Yet what evidence implicated him? Basil Hallward had left the house at eleven. Nobody had seen him return. Most of the servants were at Selby Royal. His valet had gone to bed.... Paris! Yes, Basil had gone to Paris on the midnight train, just as he had planned. Given his oddly private habits, months would pass before anyone grew suspicious. Months! Every trace could be destroyed long before that.

Suddenly an idea came to him. He put on his fur coat and hat and stepped into the hall. There he stopped, hearing a policeman's slow, heavy footsteps on the pavement outside and seeing the beam of his lantern reflected in the window. He waited, holding his breath.

A few moments later he lifted the latch and slipped outside, closing the door very softly behind him. Then he started ringing the bell.
